title: 𝒯axoSAE: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders through Taxonomic Logic

paper.title: 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders through Taxonomic Logic
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the representations of large language models (LLMs) into interpretable features, enabling precise readout and control of encoded knowledge.
However, existing SAEs treat each feature as a standalone unit, whereas real-world knowledge is often taxonomically organized.
As a result, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency, and control lacks the granularity to specify the scope of an edit.
We propose 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, which explicitly encodes taxonomical information, built on is-a (hypernym–hyponym) relations, into the SAE feature space. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE mirrors a taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, and introduces a taxonomic alignment loss that trains each concept to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is.
On two factual QA taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE enables (1) more accurate readout through the taxonomy with concentrated activations, e.g., +31.3 points in reading out the hypernyms of abstract concepts never queried in training; (2) more precise control, with +25.5 points in swap success, while suppressing a concept removes only its own answers (0–2% accuracy vs. 91–100% on other concepts); and, more importantly, (3) readout of unseen concepts through their hypernyms, with up to +37.9 points in hypernym readout accuracy. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge in their internal representations ( Sun et al., 2024a ; Cohen et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) and have achieved strong performance on a wide range of knowledge-intensive tasks ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Yifei et al., 2026 ) . However, the internal representations of LLMs remain largely opaque ( Bereska and Gavves, 2024 ; Sharkey et al., 2025 ) , making it difficult to read out what knowledge they encode and to precisely control it ( Chang et al., 2024 ; Cohen et al., 2024 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) . To mitigate this limitation, some recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn disentangled feature spaces by explicitly aligning known concepts with SAE features ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Härle et al., 2026 ) . Similarly, contrastive activation differences ( Ferrando et al., 2025 ; Yeo et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) are used with unsupervised SAEs to identify features for specific semantic information. These approaches enable more precise interpretation that can read out specific semantic information, and more targeted control via feature interventions. Despite this progress, most prior work ignores dependencies between features, leading to a flat feature space where features are not logically linked . This limits readout and control in realistic scenarios, where the knowledge is not flat, but often taxonomically organized. For example, in biology ( Diehl et al., 2011 ) , knowledge about cell types follows taxonomic logic: a T cell is a type of lymphocyte, and a lymphocyte is a type of immune cell. In such domains, one often needs to look beyond final answers to their underlying taxonomy, e.g., checking whether an LLM identifies an unfamiliar cell type as an immune cell, and sometimes to control knowledge through this taxonomy, e.g., suppressing knowledge of lymphocytes and all their subtypes without affecting other immune cells. Specifically, a flat feature space limits SAEs in two ways. First, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency : features are isolated, so readout yields disconnected activations, e.g., a T cell feature may activate while the lymphocyte feature stays silent. Second, control lacks granularity : a flat space has no notion of an edit’s scale or scope, so one cannot specify whether an edit should be minor or substantial, or which dependent information should stay unchanged. For example, replacing T cell with B cell is a minor edit that keeps it a lymphocyte, whereas replacing it with neuron is a substantial one that also changes its hypernyms, yet a flat space treats both as the same feature swap. To bridge this gap, we propose to encode taxonomical logic directly into the feature space . We introduce 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE with two components: (1) Stacked SAEs . 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE mirrors the taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, ordered from the most specific to the most abstract concepts. The first SAE reads the LLM representation and maps it onto the most specific concepts, and each higher SAE reads the reconstruction of the SAE below and maps it onto its hypernyms. (2) Taxonomic alignment loss . To realize the is-a logic (i.e., hyponym-hypernym) between the stacked SAEs, we link concept activations across levels through a training loss: a concept is trained to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. This turns the rule “if a concept holds, its hypernym holds” into a training objective. Further, this simplifies training considerably, as 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE requires explicit data points only for terminal concepts, given the taxonomy. Empirically, on two taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE yields cleaner, more readable and more controllable features than the baselines under three evaluations. (i) Readout: with concentrated activations (1.0–1.7 slots per abstract concept), readout accuracy on questions about abstract concepts never seen in training is +31.3 percentage points over the strongest baseline. (ii) Control: editing the feature of a concept steers the model’s answer to another concept with +25.5 percentage points in success, and suppressing it removes only that concept’s answers, with 0–2% accuracy against 91–100% on other concepts. (iii) Unseen concepts: for concepts absent from training, the upper levels still place them under the right hypernym, with up to +37.9 percentage points in accuracy. Our contributions are as follows: • We identify a misalignment between SAE feature spaces and the structure of real-world knowledge: while knowledge is often taxonomically organized, SAE features are not aligned with it, leaving readout without taxonomic consistency and control without granularity. • We propose 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to explicitly encode a target taxonomy into the SAE feature space. It mirrors a taxonomy with stacked SAEs and turns the is-a rule into a taxonomic alignment loss, requiring supervision only on terminal concepts. It outperforms all baselines in taxonomy readout, control. • 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE generalizes: it reads out unseen concepts at their hypernyms, whose is-a relations are absent from the SAEs’ supervision; e.g., with honeybee bound but beetle unseen, beetle questions still activate the insect slot, the baselines rarely read them as insect. This improves data efficiency, as not every concept needs binding, and suggests alignment with the taxonomy.

sections.heading: Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Alignment.
sections.text: SAEs decompose LLM representations into an overcomplete dictionary of sparse features ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Huben et al., 2024 ) , and have been scaled to large models ( Gao et al., 2025 ) with improved activation functions ( Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . Since they are trained without supervision ( Mudide et al., 2025 ; Bussmann et al., 2025 ; Muchane et al., 2025 ) , linking a feature to a concept requires post-hoc selection, e.g., by contrastive analysis of activations ( Yeo et al., 2025 ; Ferrando et al., 2025 ) , and a single concept is often split across many features or absorbed into more specific ones ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) . Accordingly, evaluations find SAE features to be imperfect units for concept readout and control ( Makelov et al., 2025 ; Karvonen et al., 2025 ) . Supervised alternatives instead bind concepts to designated units ( Koh et al., 2020 ) , and AlignSAE ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and G-SAE ( Härle et al., 2026 ) apply this to SAEs by binding each concept to a dedicated SAE slot via a supervised loss. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE builds on this slot binding, but whereas their slots are standalone, it organizes them into levels linked by is-a relations.

sections.heading: Taxonomic Knowledge in LLMs.
sections.text: LLMs encode substantial factual knowledge in their internal representations ( Sun et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2025 ) , much of which is organized by taxonomies and underlies tasks such as scholarly question answering ( Yifei et al., 2026 ) , cell type annotation ( Hou and Ji, 2024 ) , and medical coding ( Soroush et al., 2024 ) . However, LLMs make errors on such knowledge, especially on the most specific concepts ( Sun et al., 2024b ) . Prior analyses show that taxonomic structure is reflected in the geometry of LLM representations ( Park et al., 2025 ) , but focus on discovering this structure rather than on reading out and controlling concepts consistently across taxonomy levels. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE makes the taxonomy explicit in the feature space, so that the concepts and hypernyms an LLM identifies can be read out, and its errors corrected by editing them.

sections.heading: Logic Rules Encoding.
sections.text: Logic rules specify constraints that a set of facts must jointly satisfy, and integrating them into neural networks improves accuracy, data efficiency, and consistency with background knowledge ( Giunchiglia et al., 2022 ; Marra et al., 2024 ) . Prior work encodes such rules as training objectives ( Hu et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2018 ) , constraints during optimization ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , or network architectures ( Li and Srikumar, 2019 ) . Following the training-objective route, our taxonomic alignment loss encodes the is-a rule “if a hyponym holds, its hypernym holds” as a soft constraint across stacked SAEs, making taxonomic knowledge readable and editable in features.

sections.heading: 3 Task Formulation
sections.text: Figure 1: A taxonomy: each edge ( a , b ) (a,b) is an is-a link from hypernym a a to hyponym b b ; dashed edges mark further levels and nodes. Gray labels: a K = 3 K=3 example from the Animal taxonomy (full taxonomy in App. A ). 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE uses one SAE per level L k L_{k} (Fig. 2 ). To formalize our setting, we consider taxonomy subsets represented as directed acyclic graphs 𝒯 = ( V , E ) \mathcal{T}=(V,E) in which each node has at most one hypernym (see Fig. 1 ). Nodes denote taxonomic elements, i.e., concepts, and edges encode immediate hyponymy: an edge ( a , b ) ∈ E (a,b)\in E indicates that a a is the hypernym of b b , and b b is a hyponym of a a . We call nodes without parents roots and those without children terminal nodes; remaining nodes are intermediate. We index the levels of the taxonomy from the bottom: L 1 L_{1} holds the terminal nodes and L K L_{K} the roots, and 𝒱 k ⊆ V \mathcal{V}_{k}\subseteq V denotes the nodes of L k L_{k} . In this work, we study factual question answering (QA) over triples ( e , r , v ) (e,r,v) , where a question specifies an entity e e and a relation r r , and the model returns the corresponding value v v . We construct two representative taxonomies: relation taxonomies over r r and entity taxonomies over e e . We call the element of the triple organized by the taxonomy the taxonomic element t t , and the other the complementary element c c . Thus, ( t , c ) = ( r , e ) (t,c)=(r,e) for relation taxonomies and ( t , c ) = ( e , r ) (t,c)=(e,r) for entity taxonomies. For example, for “How many years does a cow typically live?” (Fig. 1 , gray, K = 3 K=3 ), the taxonomic element is t = t= cow , together with its hypernyms mammal and vertebrate , and the complementary element is c = c= typical lifespan . Figure 2: Overview of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE. We train stacked SAEs on a frozen LLM’s last-token hidden state. (1) Stacked SAEs: one SAE per taxonomy level ( L 1 , … , K L_{1,\dots,K} in Fig. 1 ), each mapping the reconstruction of the level below onto its hypernyms. (2) Taxonomic alignment loss: each taxonomic slot is trained to fire when the input involves its node or any of the node’s hyponyms. Complement slots bind the complementary element; reconstruction, sparsity, and orthogonality losses complete the objective. Figure 8 shows the full slot layout of each level on both taxonomies.

sections.heading: 4.1 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE Architecture
sections.text: To interpret the hidden states of a frozen LLM as an explicit taxonomy, we build a stack of SAEs that encode the hidden state at a given layer of the LLM. Since the last input token summarizes the prompt ( Lindsey et al., 2025 ; Afzal et al., 2025 ) , we follow AlignSAE ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and take the hidden state at this position before the first output token. Formally, given a frozen LLM M θ M_{\theta} with hidden dimension d d and input q = [ q 1 , … , q n ] q=[q_{1},\dots,q_{n}] , the input to the SAE stack is h ( 0 ) ∈ ℝ d h^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , the layer- l l hidden state of M θ M_{\theta} at the last token q n q_{n} ( l l set per dataset).

sections.heading: Stacking SAEs along the Taxonomy.
sections.text: 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE mirrors the taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one SAE per taxonomy level, ordered from the terminal to the top-level nodes (Fig. 2 ). The k k -th SAE, SAE k \mathrm{SAE}_{k} , models level L k L_{k} of the taxonomy (§ 3 and Fig. 1 ): SAE 1 \mathrm{SAE}_{1} reads the LLM hidden state and binds the terminal nodes, and each higher SAE k \mathrm{SAE}_{k} reads the reconstruction of SAE k − 1 \mathrm{SAE}_{k-1} and binds the nodes of L k L_{k} . Moving up the stack thus abstracts the representation of a question from its terminal node to the node’s hypernyms. Adjacent levels are connected by hyponymy relations, which we encode as a training loss (§ 4.2 ). Writing Enc k \mathrm{Enc}_{k} and Dec k \mathrm{Dec}_{k} for the encoder and decoder of SAE k \mathrm{SAE}_{k} , z ( k ) z^{(k)} for its feature vector, and h ( k ) h^{(k)} for its reconstruction, the stack is h ( 0 ) → Enc 1 z ( 1 ) → Dec 1 h ( 1 ) → Enc 2 ⋯ → Enc K z ( K ) → Dec K h ( K ) . h^{(0)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Enc}_{1}}z^{(1)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Dec}_{1}}h^{(1)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Enc}_{2}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Enc}_{K}}z^{(K)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Dec}_{K}}h^{(K)}.

sections.heading: Binding Taxonomic and Complementary Elements.
sections.text: Following AlignSAE ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , which binds each concept to a dedicated feature ( slot ) through post-training, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE binds taxonomic elements to slots. A question, however, has more than one semantic dimension: it gives both the taxonomic element t t and the complementary element c c of a triple ( e , r , v ) (e,r,v) (§ 3 ). For example, “How many years does a cow typically live?” asks about both the entity cow ( t t ) and the relation typical lifespan ( c c ). For a more flexible representation space, we bind both and separate them by mapping the input of each SAE k \mathrm{SAE}_{k} onto three types of slots: taxonomic slots , one per node at taxonomy level L k L_{k} ; complement slots , one per possible complementary element c c ; and unsupervised free slots for the rest of the reconstruction. sections.text: We train the encoders, decoders and value heads of all SAEs jointly. sections.heading: 5.1 Datasets and Baselines
sections.text: Datasets. We construct two factual QA datasets: (1) Bio , a relation taxonomy over biographical attributes of person names, whose terminal relations come from Freebase ( Bollacker et al., 2008 ) , with 18 terminal, 6 intermediate, and 3 top-level nodes; and (2) Animal , an entity taxonomy over animal names from an IsA subset of ConceptNet ( Speer et al., 2017 ) , with 18 terminal, 6 intermediate, and 2 top-level nodes. Training and OOD questions differ in templates (Bio) or synonyms (Animal). For example, “Who is Ralph Powers’s father?” becomes “Name Mr. Ralph Stephen Powers’s father.” at test time (Bio), and bat becomes flittermouse (Animal). See App. A for details and statistics. Baselines. We compare 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE with three baselines built on the same three-SAE stack, differing in how they assign a slot or feature to each element: (1) Random Unsup. SAE assigns each element a fixed feature by index or at random, averaged over four assignments. (2) DiffMean Unsup. SAE uses the same SAEs and picks, for each concept, the feature in its level’s SAE whose mean activation exceeds every other concept’s at that level by the largest margin, via difference-in-means ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . (3) Hybrid SAE uses the frozen terminal-level slots of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE and DiffMean-selected features from unsupervised SAEs at non-terminal levels. Unsupervised SAEs use only reconstruction and L1 losses (App. J ). A flat AlignSAE with non-terminal labels only matches our readout, swaps far worse (5.5% vs. 84.7%), and fails to keep levels consistent (0% vs. 100%; App. G ).

sections.text: Figure 3: t-SNE of L 2 L_{2} activations on Animal, colored by L 2 L_{2} node: squares are trained animals, triangles unseen ones. A triangle inside its color’s contour is placed under the right hypernym. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE does this for most unseen animals; DiffMean’s regions overlap. Mollusc is omitted due to heavy overlap in the baseline ( App. C ). Figure 4: Normalized activations ( L 1 L_{1} / L 2 L_{2} ) and binding matrices ( L 1 L_{1} – L 3 L_{3} ) on Bio. Rows group questions by their terminal node and its hypernyms. Wide panels show activations over all units: the unsupervised SAE spreads each concept over many features, while 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE concentrates it in bind slots. Square panels show each concept’s assigned unit; a diagonal means perfect binding, and “acc.” is the binding accuracy. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE enables more accurate taxonomy readout. In Table 1 , 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE matches or exceeds all baselines in Diagonal Acc on both datasets, as on Bio with Qwen2.5-0.5B (App. B ). On terminal-level questions, it reads terminal nodes and hypernyms accurately at all levels ( L 1 → L 1 / L 2 / L 3 L_{1}{\to}L_{1}/L_{2}/L_{3} ). More importantly, though trained only on terminal-level questions, it generalizes to non-terminal questions, identifying queried elements and their hypernyms. For L 2 → L 2 L_{2}{\to}L_{2} and L 3 → L 3 L_{3}{\to}L_{3} , it beats the strongest baseline by up to 25.4 points. For hypernym readout ( L 2 → L 3 L_{2}{\to}L_{3} ), it gains 31.3 points. sections.text: We test 24 animals outside the trained ones (App. C ). 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE maps most of them into the L 2 L_{2} region of their class (Fig. 3 ) and reads the right intermediate and top-level node for 63.9% and 76.1% of questions, against 26.0% and 56.8% for DiffMean. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE activations are the most concentrated.

sections.heading: 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE produces clean and concentrated activations.
sections.text: Figure 4 visualizes how terminal-level questions activate taxonomic elements on Bio. In the unsupervised SAE, each question activates many features, and the same features fire on questions about different elements, so no single feature marks an element. In 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, the taxonomic slots respond selectively: a question activates mainly the slot of its own element, at both L 1 L_{1} and L 2 L_{2} . Its binding matrices are diagonal at all three levels: questions about an element, or about any of its hyponyms, activate that element’s slot and few others. The concentration metrics in Table 1 , computed on the activations without post-hoc feature selection: 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE reaches non-terminal EffFeat of 1.0–1.7 and Top1C of 89.0–100.0%, i.e., each abstract concept is carried by about one taxonomic slot, which holds most of its activation, so a single slot suffices to read out or edit the concept; whereas the activations of unsupervised SAEs are fragmented at all three levels (Fig. 5 ).

sections.heading: Ablation Variants and Readout–Controllability Metrics.
sections.text: To assess each training loss, we evaluate five ablation variants on Bio, each removing one loss from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE. Readout averages all Test A diagonal accuracies ( L 1 → L 1 / L 2 / L 3 L_{1}{\to}L_{1}/L_{2}/L_{3} , L 2 → L 2 / L 3 L_{2}{\to}L_{2}/L_{3} , L 3 → L 3 L_{3}{\to}L_{3} ), weighted by question counts; controllability averages Test B strict accuracy and Test C target-only coverage on pairs from different top-level nodes, each at its best α \alpha . Figure 7 plots both (upper right is better); full results for Tests A–E are provided in App. F .

sections.heading: Removing any of the five losses weakens 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE’s joint readout and steering performance.
sections.text: Figure 7 shows that (1) removing taxonomic alignment ( w/o taxo align ) collapses both diagonal accuracy and swap success to the level of the random baseline; (2) removing complement alignment or value prediction ( w/o comp align , w/o value ) preserves relatively high readout accuracy but markedly reduces swap success; and (3) removing either orthogonality loss ( w/o ortho-tc , w/o ortho-tf ) shows a similar pattern, with smaller drops in swap success than other variants, while readout remains comparable and some concentration metrics improve. Replacing the bilinear value head with a per-slot head mainly weakens intermediate-level swaps (App. F.2 ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We identified that existing SAEs learn a flat feature space, which leaves readout without taxonomic consistency and control without granularity. We therefore encode taxonomic is-a logic into the feature space and propose 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, which combines stacked SAEs with a taxonomic alignment loss. On two factual QA taxonomies, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE enables more accurate taxonomy readout and more precise control than the baselines. Moreover, it reads out unseen concepts at their hypernyms without binding them, which improves data efficiency and suggests that its features align well with the taxonomy. Future work could extend it to larger models and logical relations beyond taxonomies.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our evaluation has several limitations. First, all experiments are in English, and we have not tested whether 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE transfers to other languages, where taxonomic knowledge may be expressed and encoded differently. Second, our taxonomies are relatively simple: although built from ConceptNet and Freebase, they have three levels with at most 18 terminal nodes.

sections.heading: Appendix A Datasets
sections.text: Both taxonomies build on existing resources, while the facts are controlled so that every answer is known, and both cross a three-level taxonomy with a set of complementary elements (Table 3 ). In Bio , the taxonomy is over biographical relations: 18 terminal relations (e.g., birth city , employer , father ) are grouped into 6 intermediate relations ( place of birth , place of death , employment , education , immediate family , extended family ) and 3 top-level relations ( life places , professional background , social relations ); the terminal relations are person relations from Freebase ( Bollacker et al., 2008 ) , and we generate the more abstract intermediate and top-level relations above them; the complementary elements are 20 synthetic people, and each person has one value for each terminal relation. In Animal , the taxonomy is over animals: 18 terminal animals (e.g., cow , frog , octopus ) are grouped into 6 intermediate classes ( mammal , bird , amphibian , fish , insect , mollusc ) and 2 top-level classes ( vertebrate , invertebrate ), forming a subset of the English IsA relations of ConceptNet ( Speer et al., 2017 ) ; the complementary elements are 20 properties (e.g., limb count , capable of flight , diet type ), and each animal has one value for each property. A non-terminal node takes, for each complementary element, the set of values of its terminal hyponyms. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE is trained only on terminal-level questions. Bio varies the question template (10 in training) and the surface form of the person’s name (4 per person); Animal varies the template (54 in training) and the animal’s synonym (5–8 per animal, 108 in total). The readout tests add held-out templates, names, or synonyms at the terminal level, and intermediate- and top-level questions, none of which appear in training. sections.heading: Appendix C Unseen Terminal Concepts
sections.text: A taxonomy should let the upper levels place a concept that no terminal slot was trained on. We ask the Animal model (layer 9) about 24 animals outside its 18 terminal concepts, four per intermediate node (e.g., pig , dog , horse , and lion for mammal ), filling the 100 question templates of a trained terminal concept with the new name, and read the SAEs as in the readout test (Table 7 ). No terminal slot fits these animals: the highest L 1 L_{1} score halves relative to the trained concepts, and 72.5% of the questions fall below the 5th percentile of the trained ones. Because the L 1 L_{1} slots are trained as an 18-way classifier without a “none” option, the weaker slot still wins most of the time, usually that of the closest sibling ( pig → \to cow , newt → \to salamander , tuna → \to salmon ). The upper levels still recover the animal’s place in the taxonomy: the L 2 L_{2} slots of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE read the right intermediate node for 63.9% of the questions and the L 3 L_{3} slots the right top-level node for 76.1%, against 26.0% and 56.8% for DiffMean Unsup. SAE. Hybrid SAE, which shares the terminal-level SAE of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, is at chance at L 2 L_{2} (16.7%), so the gain comes from the supervised upper levels rather than from the L 1 L_{1} read; when L 1 L_{1} points to a terminal concept under another intermediate node, the L 2 L_{2} slots of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE still read the right intermediate node for 31.1% of the questions, against 1.4% for Hybrid SAE. Errors concentrate on a few animals ( sparrow , owl , goldfish , cod , ant , slug ), while 12 of the 24 animals are classified correctly for at least 99% of their questions. On Bio, the terminal concepts are relations, so we add 24 relations outside the 18 trained terminal relations, four under each intermediate relation (e.g., uncle , aunt , nephew , and niece under extended family ), each asked about the 20 people with five question templates. Table 6 lists all unseen concepts. The L 1 L_{1} slots again do not fit them (98.0% of the questions fall below the 5th percentile of the trained ones), while the upper levels of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE read the right intermediate relation for 91.4% of the questions and the right top-level relation for 94.8%, against 75.9% and 69.8% for the strongest baselines (Table 7 ). Errors concentrate on advisor , which is mostly read as immediate family (its questions ask “who is X’s advisor”, like the family relations), and on uncle , nephew , and niece , which are partly read as immediate family or abstained on. sections.heading: Appendix G Flat AlignSAE Baseline
sections.text: To test whether the stack is needed, we train a flat AlignSAE ( Yang et al., 2025 ) that binds all levels in a single SAE (Fig. 11 ). It reads h ( 0 ) h^{(0)} directly and has one taxonomic slot for every node of every level, 20 complement slots, and 10,000 free slots. Each level’s group of taxonomic slots is supervised with that level’s label of the question, derived from the taxonomy, with no stacking and no derived ( is-a ) targets. All other losses, weights, and the two-stage schedule (100 + 500 epochs) follow 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, and the tests are run in the same way, editing the slots of the swapped level only. Table 12 reports the results on Bio (layer 6). Readout is close to that of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE: both read terminal-level questions perfectly at every level, and the flat SAE reads non-terminal questions about as well. Control is far weaker. A terminal swap succeeds for only 5.5% of the questions, against 84.7% for 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE: editing a terminal slot leaves the intermediate and top-level slots of the same SAE on the source concept, so after a swap across intermediate nodes the flat SAE still reads the source’s intermediate node in every case. In 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, the edited reconstruction feeds the higher SAEs, which read the target’s intermediate node in every case. The intermediate swap shows the same gap (18.3% vs. 41.8%), and the flat SAE never reads the target’s top-level node, since editing its intermediate slot leaves its top-level slots unchanged. Supervision alone thus suffices for readout, while consistent control across levels requires the stacked structure. sections.text: In the readout test (Test A), a read counts as wrong when the most active unit is not clearly ahead, i.e., its activation exceeds the second highest by less than 10%. A swap encodes the hidden state with the SAE of the edited level, sets the unit of the source node to 0 and that of the target node to the strength α \alpha , and decodes. For a terminal-level swap the edit is made in SAE 1 \mathrm{SAE}_{1} ; for an intermediate-level swap the hidden state is passed through SAE 1 \mathrm{SAE}_{1} and the edit is made in SAE 2 \mathrm{SAE}_{2} . On Bio, swaps follow § 5.3 : only the last prompt token is edited, and its hidden state is replaced with the decoded state Dec ⁡ ( z ′ ) \mathrm{Dec}(z^{\prime}) . sections.text: Table 13 reports answer performance and taxonomic readout after steering on Bio and Animal, with each system evaluated at its best steering strength α \alpha . Terminal-level swaps cover all source–target pairs, while intermediate-level swaps use pairs from different top-level nodes. In addition to target-answer metrics, we evaluate whether the edited activations encode the target element’s hypernyms. After terminal-level swaps, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE achieves 100% intermediate-level readout on both datasets and top-level readout of 93.2% on Bio and 99.2% on Animal. After intermediate-level swaps, top-level readout reaches 100% on both datasets. Although Hybrid SAE shares the same terminal-level answer performance, its non-terminal readout is substantially weaker. These results show that steering with 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE aligns higher-level readout with the target element, even when the generated answer does not always match the target.

Morrison Affiliation: University of Arizona Email: eduardoblanco@arizona.edu Eduardo Blanco Mihai Surdeanu Affiliation: University of Arizona Email: msurdeanu@arizona.edu Email: minglai.yang@scale.com Abstract Recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the representations of large language models (LLMs) into interpretable features, enabling precise readout and control of encoded knowledge. However, existing SAEs treat each feature as a standalone unit, whereas real-world knowledge is often taxonomically organized. As a result, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency, and control lacks the granularity to specify the scope of an edit. We propose 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, which explicitly encodes taxonomical information, built on is-a (hypernym–hyponym) relations, into the SAE feature space. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE mirrors a taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, and introduces a taxonomic alignment loss that trains each concept to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. On two factual QA taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE enables (1) more accurate readout through the taxonomy with concentrated activations, e.g., +31.3 points in reading out the hypernyms of abstract concepts never queried in training; (2) more precise control, with +25.5 points in swap success, while suppressing a concept removes only its own answers (0–2% accuracy vs. 91–100% on other concepts); and, more importantly, (3) readout of unseen concepts through their hypernyms, with up to +37.9 points in hypernym readout accuracy. GitHub 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge in their internal representations ( Sun et al., 2024a ; Cohen et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) and have achieved strong performance on a wide range of knowledge-intensive tasks ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Yifei et al., 2026 ) . However, the internal representations of LLMs remain largely opaque ( Bereska and Gavves, 2024 ; Sharkey et al., 2025 ) , making it difficult to read out what knowledge they encode and to precisely control it ( Chang et al., 2024 ; Cohen et al., 2024 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) . To mitigate this limitation, some recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn disentangled feature spaces by explicitly aligning known concepts with SAE features ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Härle et al., 2026 ) . Similarly, contrastive activation differences ( Ferrando et al., 2025 ; Yeo et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) are used with unsupervised SAEs to identify features for specific semantic information. These approaches enable more precise interpretation that can read out specific semantic information, and more targeted control via feature interventions. Despite this progress, most prior work ignores dependencies between features, leading to a flat feature space where features are not logically linked . This limits readout and control in realistic scenarios, where the knowledge is not flat, but often taxonomically organized. For example, in biology ( Diehl et al., 2011 ) , knowledge about cell types follows taxonomic logic: a T cell is a type of lymphocyte, and a lymphocyte is a type of immune cell. In such domains, one often needs to look beyond final answers to their underlying taxonomy, e.g., checking whether an LLM identifies an unfamiliar cell type as an immune cell, and sometimes to control knowledge through this taxonomy, e.g., suppressing knowledge of lymphocytes and all their subtypes without affecting other immune cells. Specifically, a flat feature space limits SAEs in two ways. First, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency : features are isolated, so readout yields disconnected activations, e.g., a T cell feature may activate while the lymphocyte feature stays silent. Second, control lacks granularity : a flat space has no notion of an edit’s scale or scope, so one cannot specify whether an edit should be minor or substantial, or which dependent information should stay unchanged. For example, replacing T cell with B cell is a minor edit that keeps it a lymphocyte, whereas replacing it with neuron is a substantial one that also changes its hypernyms, yet a flat space treats both as the same feature swap. To bridge this gap, we propose to encode taxonomical logic directly into the feature space . We introduce 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE with two components: (1) Stacked SAEs . 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE mirrors the taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, ordered from the most specific to the most abstract concepts. The first SAE reads the LLM representation and maps it onto the most specific concepts, and each higher SAE reads the reconstruction of the SAE below and maps it onto its hypernyms. (2) Taxonomic alignment loss . To realize the is-a logic (i.e., hyponym-hypernym) between the stacked SAEs, we link concept activations across levels through a training loss: a concept is trained to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. This turns the rule “if a concept holds, its hypernym holds” into a training objective. Further, this simplifies training considerably, as 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE requires explicit data points only for terminal concepts, given the taxonomy. Empirically, on two taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE yields cleaner, more readable and more controllable features than the baselines under three evaluations. (i) Readout: with concentrated activations (1.0–1.7 slots per abstract concept), readout accuracy on questions about abstract concepts never seen in training is +31.3 percentage points over the strongest baseline. (ii) Control: editing the feature of a concept steers the model’s answer to another concept with +25.5 percentage points in success, and suppressing it removes only that concept’s answers, with 0–2% accuracy against 91–100% on other concepts. (iii) Unseen concepts: for concepts absent from training, the upper levels still place them under the right hypernym, with up to +37.9 percentage points in accuracy. Our contributions are as follows: • We identify a misalignment between SAE feature spaces and the structure of real-world knowledge: while knowledge is often taxonomically organized, SAE features are not aligned with it, leaving readout without taxonomic consistency and control without granularity. • We propose 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to explicitly encode a target taxonomy into the SAE feature space. It mirrors a taxonomy with stacked SAEs and turns the is-a rule into a taxonomic alignment loss, requiring supervision only on terminal concepts. It outperforms all baselines in taxonomy readout, control. • 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE generalizes: it reads out unseen concepts at their hypernyms, whose is-a relations are absent from the SAEs’ supervision; e.g., with honeybee bound but beetle unseen, beetle questions still activate the insect slot, the baselines rarely read them as insect. This improves data efficiency, as not every concept needs binding, and suggests alignment with the taxonomy. 2 Related Work Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Alignment. SAEs decompose LLM representations into an overcomplete dictionary of sparse features ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Huben et al., 2024 ) , and have been scaled to large models ( Gao et al., 2025 ) with improved activation functions ( Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . Since they are trained without supervision ( Mudide et al., 2025 ; Bussmann et al., 2025 ; Muchane et al., 2025 ) , linking a feature to a concept requires post-hoc selection, e.g., by contrastive analysis of activations ( Yeo et al., 2025 ; Ferrando et al., 2025 ) , and a single concept is often split across many features or absorbed into more specific ones ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) . Accordingly, evaluations find SAE features to be imperfect units for concept readout and control ( Makelov et al., 2025 ; Karvonen et al., 2025 ) . Supervised alternatives instead bind concepts to designated units ( Koh et al., 2020 ) , and AlignSAE ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and G-SAE ( Härle et al., 2026 ) apply this to SAEs by binding each concept to a dedicated SAE slot via a supervised loss. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE builds on this slot binding, but whereas their slots are standalone, it organizes them into levels linked by is-a relations. Taxonomic Knowledge in LLMs. LLMs encode substantial factual knowledge in their internal representations ( Sun et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2025 ) , much of which is organized by taxonomies and underlies tasks such as scholarly question answering ( Yifei et al., 2026 ) , cell type annotation ( Hou and Ji, 2024 ) , and medical coding ( Soroush et al., 2024 ) . However, LLMs make errors on such knowledge, especially on the most specific concepts ( Sun et al., 2024b ) . Prior analyses show that taxonomic structure is reflected in the geometry of LLM representations ( Park et al., 2025 ) , but focus on discovering this structure rather than on reading out and controlling concepts consistently across taxonomy levels. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE makes the taxonomy explicit in the feature space, so that the concepts and hypernyms an LLM identifies can be read out, and its errors corrected by editing them. Logic Rules Encoding. Logic rules specify constraints that a set of facts must jointly satisfy, and integrating them into neural networks improves accuracy, data efficiency, and consistency with background knowledge ( Giunchiglia et al., 2022 ; Marra et al., 2024 ) . Prior work encodes such rules as training objectives ( Hu et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2018 ) , constraints during optimization ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , or network architectures ( Li and Srikumar, 2019 ) . Following the training-objective route, our taxonomic alignment loss encodes the is-a rule “if a hyponym holds, its hypernym holds” as a soft constraint across stacked SAEs, making taxonomic knowledge readable and editable in features. 3 Task Formulation Figure 1: A taxonomy: each edge ( a , b ) (a,b) is an is-a link from hypernym a a to hyponym b b ; dashed edges mark further levels and nodes. Gray labels: a K = 3 K=3 example from the Animal taxonomy (full taxonomy in App. A ). 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE uses one SAE per level L k L_{k} (Fig. 2 ). To formalize our setting, we consider taxonomy subsets represented as directed acyclic graphs 𝒯 = ( V , E ) \mathcal{T}=(V,E) in which each node has at most one hypernym (see Fig. 1 ). Nodes denote taxonomic elements, i.e., concepts, and edges encode immediate hyponymy: an edge ( a , b ) ∈ E (a,b)\in E indicates that a a is the hypernym of b b , and b b is a hyponym of a a . We call nodes without parents roots and those without children terminal nodes; remaining nodes are intermediate. We index the levels of the taxonomy from the bottom: L 1 L_{1} holds the terminal nodes and L K L_{K} the roots, and 𝒱 k ⊆ V \mathcal{V}_{k}\subseteq V denotes the nodes of L k L_{k} . In this work, we study factual question answering (QA) over triples ( e , r , v ) (e,r,v) , where a question specifies an entity e e and a relation r r , and the model returns the corresponding value v v . We construct two representative taxonomies: relation taxonomies over r r and entity taxonomies over e e . We call the element of the triple organized by the taxonomy the taxonomic element t t , and the other the complementary element c c . Thus, ( t , c ) = ( r , e ) (t,c)=(r,e) for relation taxonomies and ( t , c ) = ( e , r ) (t,c)=(e,r) for entity taxonomies. For example, for “How many years does a cow typically live?” (Fig. 1 , gray, K = 3 K=3 ), the taxonomic element is t = t= cow , together with its hypernyms mammal and vertebrate , and the complementary element is c = c= typical lifespan . Figure 2: Overview of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE. We train stacked SAEs on a frozen LLM’s last-token hidden state. (1) Stacked SAEs: one SAE per taxonomy level ( L 1 , … , K L_{1,\dots,K} in Fig. 1 ), each mapping the reconstruction of the level below onto its hypernyms. (2) Taxonomic alignment loss: each taxonomic slot is trained to fire when the input involves its node or any of the node’s hyponyms. Complement slots bind the complementary element; reconstruction, sparsity, and orthogonality losses complete the objective. Figure 8 shows the full slot layout of each level on both taxonomies. 4 Method 4.1 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE Architecture To interpret the hidden states of a frozen LLM as an explicit taxonomy, we build a stack of SAEs that encode the hidden state at a given layer of the LLM. We therefore encode taxonomic is-a logic into the feature space and propose 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE, which combines stacked SAEs with a taxonomic alignment loss. On two factual QA taxonomies, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE enables more accurate taxonomy readout and more precise control than the baselines. Moreover, it reads out unseen concepts at their hypernyms without binding them, which improves data efficiency and suggests that its features align well with the taxonomy. Future work could extend it to larger models and logical relations beyond taxonomies. Limitations Our evaluation has several limitations. First, all experiments are in English, and we have not tested whether 𝒯 \mathcal{T} axoSAE transfers to other languages, where taxonomic knowledge may be expressed and encoded differently.
